title: How Container Ship Crews Eat, Shower & Sleep for Months at Sea
asof: Rules from MLC 2006 · survey data as of 2025 · sources in description

shots.s: This ship is about as long as four football fields.
It carries thousands of containers.
And only about twenty-five people.
They stay on board for months.
Sometimes they don't step ashore for weeks.
So how do you eat,
shower,
and sleep,
on a container ship?
The biggest container ships are about four hundred meters long.
When the Ever Given got stuck in the Suez Canal in 2021,
it had a crew of twenty-five.
Almost everything you buy has been on a ship like this.
Up front: containers, stacked high.
At the back: the engine room,
and a tall white tower called the accommodation.
That's where the crew lives.
Bridge on top.
Cabins, galley, mess room and gym below.
A ship never stops.
So the crew works in watches, around the clock.
There's a rule for rest.
The Maritime Labour Convention says:
at least ten hours of rest in any twenty-four.
At least seventy-seven hours in any seven days.
In port, everyone works harder.
Cranes load and unload day and night.
A cook feeds the whole crew.
Food comes aboard in port,
and has to last until the next one.
Each ship gets a set food budget per person.
In 2025, a seafarers' survey found that food quality was falling.
Food prices rose, but budgets didn't.
One crew member described the food as too much, but not tasty.
Meals matter a lot out here.
The survey called them one of the few daily pleasures on board.
Most crew get their own cabin.
A bed, a desk, a small bathroom.
The shower is fresh water, made on board from seawater.
In rough seas, the whole ship rolls.
You wedge yourself into your bed to sleep.
And the engine hums through the steel, all day, all night.
Weeks at sea, with the same faces.
Shore leave used to be the escape.
In the 2025 survey, shore leave scored lowest of everything.
Port stays are short.
There are inspections and audits.
And transport into town can cost a lot.
Many crew stay on board for the whole port call.
Internet is the lifeline.
Some ships have good connections.
Others have tiny data allowances.
For a seafarer, calling home means everything.
Some routes pass through pirate waters.
So many ships have a citadel.
A locked safe room the crew can retreat to.
Guidance says it should hold food and water for at least three days.
In November 2025, pirates boarded a tanker off Somalia.
All twenty-four crew locked themselves in the citadel.
The pirates gave up and left.
Everyone was safe.
Contracts often run six to nine months.
The rules say no more than eleven months on board without leave.
In 2020, COVID broke that system.
Borders closed, and crews couldn't be swapped.
By December 2020, the UN shipping agency said over four hundred thousand seafarers were stuck at sea.
Many past the end of their contracts.
Then one day, your replacement walks up the gangway.
You hand over your job.
And you go home.
Someone else takes your cabin.
And the ship sails on.
Could you spend nine months on a ship with twenty-five people?
